_note: Condition cards are DATA. A medic can change a limit or T_harm here without touching code. Every T_harm marked assumption: true is an ASSUMPTION for the prototype, not a medical standard.

cards.name: Fever with fast heart rate
cards.plain: Your temperature is high and your heart is beating fast at rest. Together these can mean your body is fighting an infection and may get worse within hours.
steps: Stop work and rest lying down in your crew quarters.
Drink 250 ml of water now and keep sipping.
Re-measure temperature and heart rate in 30 minutes.
Ask a crewmate to stay nearby and check on you.
cards.escalation: Tell the Crew Medical Officer (CMO) now. The CMO decides what to do next using the on-board medical guide.
redFlags: Stiff neck or a rash that does not fade when pressed

cards.name: Fever
cards.plain: Your temperature is 38 °C or higher. A fever usually means an infection; in space your immune system may be weaker than on Earth.
steps: Rest and drink fluids.
Note any other symptoms: cough, sore throat, rash, pain.
Re-measure in 2 hours.
Keep a little distance from crewmates until it settles.
cards.escalation: Tell the CMO today. If it rises above 39 °C, tell the CMO straight away.

cards.name: Very high blood pressure
cards.plain: Blood pressure this high can strain the heart and brain quickly.
steps: Sit still, breathe slowly for 5 minutes.
Re-measure after 5 minutes on the other arm.
cards.escalation: Tell the CMO now, even if you feel fine.
redFlags: Very bad headache or blurred vision
Weak or numb on one side, trouble speaking

sources.title: American Heart Association: When to call 911 about high blood pressure

cards.name: High blood pressure
cards.plain: Your blood pressure is in the high range. It is not an emergency on its own, but it should come down over the next days.
steps: Rest 10 minutes and re-measure.
Keep salt low and drink your water ration.
Protect tonight's sleep.
Do your planned aerobic exercise.
cards.escalation: Tell the CMO today and re-measure every 4 hours.
redFlags: Very bad headache or blurred vision

sources.title: American Heart Association: Understanding blood pressure readings

cards.name: Low blood oxygen
cards.plain: Your blood is carrying less oxygen than it should. This can come from the cabin air or from your lungs.
steps: Check the cabin O₂/CO₂ display.
Sit upright and breathe slowly and deeply.
Re-measure in 5 minutes with warm hands.
cards.escalation: Tell the CMO now. If the cabin air is fine, the CMO decides on oxygen using the on-board guide.

sources.title: MedlinePlus: Pulse oximetry (contact a provider at 92 % or lower)

cards.name: Low blood sugar
cards.plain: Your blood sugar is very low. It can make you shaky, confused or faint within minutes.
steps: Eat or drink 15 g of fast sugar now (a juice pouch).
Re-measure in 15 minutes.
Eat a proper snack once it is back above 70 mg/dL.

sources.title: American Diabetes Association (2025) Standards of Care: hypoglycaemia levels 1 and 2

cards.name: Very slow heart rate
cards.plain: Your resting heart rate is very slow. In fit people it can be normal, but with dizziness it needs attention.
steps: Lie down.
Re-measure in 10 minutes.
cards.escalation: Tell the CMO now if you feel dizzy or faint.

cards.name: Severe sleep loss
cards.plain: You slept less than 5 hours. Your reactions and judgement are slower today.
steps: No safety-critical tasks (EVA, docking, piloting) today.
Lights out at 22:00, no screens for an hour before.
No caffeine after 14:00.
Crew check-in: talk with a crewmate.
cards.escalation: Tell the CMO and the commander so the schedule can change on board.

sources.title: Watson et al. (2015) Recommended amount of sleep for a healthy adult

cards.name: Very low mood
cards.plain: Your mood is very low. Long isolation and distance from home make this common, and it gets better with support.
steps: Talk to a crewmate today.
Record a message to family for the next link window.
Do 20 minutes of exercise you enjoy.
Keep a regular sleep time.
cards.escalation: Tell the commander or CMO today. Use the buddy system.

sources.title: NASA Human Research Program: Hazards of human spaceflight

unusual.name: Unusual day for you
unusual.plain: Several of your readings are each a little off at the same time. On their own none would set off an alarm, but together they are unusual for you.
steps: Re-measure the flagged readings in 2 hours.
Note any symptoms (feeling hot, aches, cough, headache).
Rest and drink water.
unusual.escalation: If anything is worse at the re-check, tell the CMO.

drift.name: Slow drift
drift.plain: One reading has been creeping in the same direction for days. No single day looks wrong, but the trend will reach the limit if it continues.
steps: Keep measuring daily at the same time.
Look at sleep, exercise, salt and stress over the same days.
Follow the recovery steps for this reading.
drift.escalation: Tell the CMO at the next medical check-in and include the trend in a Consult Packet.
